clue.text: Sauce and beans occasionally found in pancake

indicators.note: something done only occasionally happens every other time, so only some of the letters are used
what is found in something sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a taco is a folded Mexican corn pancake
the first, third and fifth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A cook adds a sauce and some beans to a pancake filling.
explanation.walkthrough: A taco is not usually called a pancake, but its soft corn tortilla is a flat griddled cake, which makes the substitution fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabasco is a proprietary brand of hot pepper sauce, so it is an example of a sauce.

clue.text: Count to play the informer

blocks.note: first meaning: to number things, as a bank teller does
second meaning: to snitch on someone

explanation.surface: A nobleman, a count, turns informer and betrays his friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a title of nobility; it is the verb meaning to number.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell is both to reckon a number (as in 'all told') and, informally, to sneak on someone to an authority.

clue.text: Impatient exclamation from Scot splitting cheese roll

indicators.note: something splitting another thing drives into its middle, so it ends up inside it

blocks.note: a soft French cheese
a Scottish cry of irritation

explanation.surface: A Scot impatiently cries out while cutting open a cheese roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheese roll' reads as one sandwich; the cheese is wordplay and the roll alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brioche is a soft enriched French bread, often baked as an individual roll.

clue.text: Beatles manager once leaving record for writer

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so those letters are dropped from the name

blocks.note: Brian Epstein managed the Beatles in the 1960s
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: The Beatles' old manager walks away from a record deal to become an author.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove EP from EPSTEIN to leave STEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude Stein was an American novelist and poet, so she is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Spontaneous occurrence before the public holiday

blocks.note: something out is open and public, known to all
a short holiday is a break

explanation.surface: Something happens unexpectedly just before a public holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: OUT then BREAK gives OUTBREAK; 'the public' stands for being out in the open.
explanation.definitionFit: An outbreak is a sudden eruption of disease, war or violence, something that flares up of its own accord.

clue.text: Measure Juliet put into pub's glass container

indicators.note: things put into something are placed inside it

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
an ell is an old measure of cloth length
Juliet is J in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A measure of drink is poured for Juliet into a glass at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' suggests a measure of spirits at the bar; here it is an old unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell jar is a bell-shaped glass cover used in laboratories and to protect displays.

clue.text: Whistler secured in bank that's robbed?

indicators.note: something secured in a place is held safely inside it

blocks.note: to bank on something is to bet on it
a referee blows the whistle

explanation.surface: A man with a whistle is locked in a bank that is being robbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' and 'robbed' paint a heist, but bank is the verb to rely on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bereft means deprived of something, as anyone robbed has been; the question mark admits the stretch.

clue.text: Debauchee having left island, knight Edward VII embraces?

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms round, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation for left
the usual abbreviation for island
Edward VII was known in the family as Bertie
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A rake has left an island where Edward VII is knighting people.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward VII was notorious as a playboy, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A libertine is a person who lives a dissolute, sexually unrestrained life, exactly a debauchee.

clue.text: The Fool — as shown in the cards?

indicators.note: something shown in a display is set within it

blocks.note: jacks are court cards in a pack
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Fool, as he appears in a tarot pack.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fool really is a tarot card, which makes the surface convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackass is a male donkey and by extension a stupid person, a fool.

clue.text: Disowned aide, put out, getting into the wine

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed and upset, so these letters are thrown into disorder
something getting into another thing ends up within it

blocks.note: red is wine
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An assistant, upset, takes to drink after being disowned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' does double duty in the surface but here is fodder, with 'out' acting as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate is to reject or refuse to acknowledge, so repudiated means disowned.

clue.text: Sheep kills time in an easterly wind

indicators.note: an easterly wind blows from the east, so in an across answer the word travels right to left
the pieces are placed within the wind word

blocks.note: to reel is to wind, as a fishing line
ices is slang for kills
the usual abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Livestock are dying in a bitter east wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as weather; it is the verb, as when winding a fishing line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leicester is a breed of English long-wool sheep, so it is an example of sheep.

clue.text: Northern town taxi turned towards a centre

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi
in British usage one goes up to the capital or a city centre

explanation.surface: A taxi in a northern town turns and heads for the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: CAB backwards is BAC, then UP. BACUP is a small mill town in Lancashire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacup is a town in Rossendale, Lancashire, in the north of England.

clue.text: Showing heart, cross about conflict, one trained to attack

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: the heart of something is its centre
to ford a river is to cross it
war is conflict

explanation.surface: A brave fighter crosses into battle, trained for the offensive.
explanation.walkthrough: A centre forward is the main striker in a football team.
explanation.definitionFit: A centre forward is the attacking player at the head of a football side, whose role is to score.

clue.text: Character billed as old and decrepit — nothing to it

indicators.note: something decrepit is broken down, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
in cricket a duck is a score of zero

explanation.surface: Someone is described as old and decrepit, worthless through and through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Billed' seems to mean advertised; it means having a bill. A duck in cricket is a batsman's score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Donald Duck is a Disney cartoon character, and being a duck he has a beak, or bill.

clue.text: Patent protecting firm — origin of Apple Mac?

indicators.note: the origin is where something begins, so only the first letter is taken
something protecting another wraps round it as a shield

blocks.note: patent means obvious, open
Co is the abbreviation for company
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A patent protects the firm behind the Apple Mac computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple Mac' suggests computers; a mac is a mackintosh raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A mac, short for mackintosh, is a waterproof coat worn over other clothes, so it is a kind of overcoat.

clue.text: Short file, kept by alliance in Somerset, that goes sideways

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so its last letter is lost
something kept by another is held within it

blocks.note: a cartel is an alliance of businesses
to file a blade is to sharpen, or whet, it

explanation.surface: A shortened document is held by a coalition in the county of Somerset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somerset' looks like the English county but is an old word for somersault.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartwheel is a gymnastic move turning the body sideways over the hands, a somersault performed side-on.

clue.text: Duke ingesting MDMA joins a celebration

indicators.note: something ingesting another takes it inside itself

blocks.note: dukes is slang for fists
MDMA is the drug ecstasy, E for short
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat takes ecstasy and joins a party.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside FIST, then A follows. 'Duke' seems to be a nobleman; 'put up your dukes' means raise your fists.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a festival or party, especially in Spanish-speaking countries.

clue.text: Outlaws part that's wrapped with note

indicators.note: the part is wrapped round the next piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: a bit is a part
and means together with
ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Criminals hand over a share wrapped up with a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a joining word but supplies letters, as 'and' means together with.
explanation.definitionFit: Banditti is the Italian-style plural of bandit, and bandits are outlaws.

clue.text: Despair initially avoided may become hope

indicators.note: the first letter is the one avoided, so it is left off
becoming something else means a change of form, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the word without its first letter

explanation.surface: If you steer clear of despair at the outset, it may turn into hope.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a neat motivational saying, and the answer is the verb, as in 'aspire to greatness'.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to set one's hopes on achieving something, so it matches hope as a verb.

clue.text: Select times for admission to A&E? That's ground-breaking!

indicators.note: being admitted to a place means going inside it

blocks.note: to pick is to select
taken as written
x is the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: Choosing when to go into hospital emergency would be a breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: A pickaxe is a digging tool used literally to break hard ground, so the exclamation is a playful definition.

clue.text: Trap a king — what's stopping merry old one?

indicators.note: something stopping a gap plugs it, sitting inside it

blocks.note: Old King Cole was a merry old soul in the nursery rhyme
taken as written
K is king in chess and cards
eh is a request to repeat, like what?

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a jolly old king is being trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' looks like a verb but is the noun: cakehole and trap are both British slang for mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Both trap and cakehole are informal British words for the mouth, as in 'shut your trap'.

clue.text: Old Greek character given support raised snakes

indicators.note: in a down answer, raising something sends it upward, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation for old
phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
aid is support

explanation.surface: A figure from ancient Greek myth is helped up by snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: O and PHI, then AID upward as DIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophidia is the zoological name for the suborder of reptiles comprising the snakes.

clue.text: Taken to beer without opening tin cans?

indicators.note: lacking its opening means the first letter is missing
cans as a verb means puts into a tin, so the pieces are enclosed

blocks.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
taken as written
ale is beer

explanation.surface: Somebody has taken to drinking beer straight from a can without opening it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cans' looks like a noun but is the verb, to seal in a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolen means taken unlawfully, so it can replace taken as a past participle.

clue.text: Take serious risks? Ditch the idea, bowling round wicket

indicators.note: bowling along means rolling briskly, so the letters are tumbled
round means surrounding, so the cricket letter is enclosed

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
W is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a wicket

explanation.surface: A cricketer is told to drop the plan of bowling round the wicket because it is too risky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowling round the wicket' is a real cricket phrase meaning delivering from the far side of the stumps, which hides the mechanics.
explanation.definitionFit: To dice with death is an idiom for behaving in a dangerously reckless way, gambling with one's life.

clue.text: Partners in crime?

blocks.note: surface reading: a noun, accomplices who commit offences together
setter's reading: a verb, one who partners another in wrongdoing by helping them

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as a plural noun for accomplices; read 'partners' as a verb and it describes helping someone commit an offence.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to encourage or assist someone in committing a crime, which is acting as their partner in it.

clue.text: Crew said something at Chiswick in Boat Race

definitions.text: something at Chiswick in Boat Race

indicators.note: said tells us the word is heard, not seen

blocks.note: a rowing crew of eight is called an eight

explanation.surface: A rowing crew talks about a landmark on the Boat Race course at Chiswick.
explanation.walkthrough: An eyot, a river island, is pronounced 'ait'. Chiswick Eyot is a Thames island passed in the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiswick Eyot is a small island in the Thames along the Boat Race course, so it is a landmark there.

clue.text: United by wise tradition

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for United in football team names
sage means wise

explanation.surface: People brought together by a wise old custom.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means established custom or practice, especially habitual ways of doing things handed down.

clue.text: Daughters in coffee bar that's contemporary

indicators.note: the letter for daughters is placed within the following word

blocks.note: a latte is a milky coffee
a bar of light is a ray
the usual abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Daughters hang out in a trendy coffee bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coffee bar' reads as a café; the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Latter-day means belonging to recent or present times, a modern version, so it is a synonym for contemporary.

clue.text: Family outside on marks close to royal citadel

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken
a word placed outside others surrounds them

blocks.note: kin are family
re means on or concerning
M is the abbreviation for marks, the old German currency
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A family stands outside the walls of a royal fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' is the old German currency, the Deutschmark, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kremlin is the fortified complex at the heart of Moscow; kremlin is Russian for a city citadel.

clue.text: Second sin St Anthony embodies?

indicators.note: something that embodies another holds it within its body

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A second sin is committed by St Anthony, the famously tempted saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' seems to qualify 'sin'; it is the definition, a short moment.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant is a very short moment of time, as is a second in everyday speech.
